name: The Life of Paul
subtitle: Acts and the letters, on one timeline
blurb: Luke tells the journeys; Paul, in his letters, tells the same years from the inside. Lay them side by side and each letter falls into its place — the city it was written from, the journey that produced it.
howToRead: Two tracks for two witnesses to the same life: above, the journeys as Luke narrates them in Acts; below, the letters Paul wrote along the way, each block set at the place and moment it was sent. Click a journey or a letter for its dossier; the diamonds on the spine are the turning-points. A dotted edge marks a date the sources leave genuinely open.
seedNote: Pauline chronology is reconstructed, not given. This edition lets you read it three ways — use the chronology switch above to move between the Acts-based consensus (anchored on Gallio's proconsulship at Corinth, c. A.D. 51), Douglas Campbell's letters-first reconstruction (anchored on the escape from Aretas's ethnarch, c. A.D. 36–37), and Gerd Lüdemann's (anchored on the time-spans of Galatians 1–2, counted from a crucifixion of A.D. 30). The two alternatives deliberately bracket Acts and build from the letters alone, so they date the letters earlier and in a different order — and they simply do not fix the Acts-only episodes (the numbered journeys, the Caesarean custody, the voyage and shipwreck, the martyrdom), which is why those blocks thin out or vanish when you switch. Each scheme's dates are drawn from that scholar's own work, but every reconstruction here remains a scholarly proposal, not a record.

lanes.name: The journeys — Acts
lanes.note: Damascus → Antioch → the three journeys → Rome

lanes.name: The letters — Paul's hand
lanes.note: each set where and when it was sent

spans.label: Damascus & Arabia
spans.aside: "I went away into Arabia… then after three years I went up to Jerusalem" (Gal 1:17–18) — Paul's own count of these years.
spans.note: After the Damascus road, three years out of sight — Arabia, then Damascus again, escaping the city in a basket lowered through the wall.

spans.label: Tarsus & Antioch
spans.aside: The silent decade — almost a third of his Christian life, barely narrated.
spans.note: Sent home to Tarsus, then fetched by Barnabas to teach at Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. Ends with the famine-relief visit to Jerusalem.

spans.label: First journey
spans.detail: Cyprus · Pisidian Antioch · Iconium · Lystra · Derbe
spans.note: Sent out by the Antioch church with Barnabas. Across Cyprus and into the highlands of Galatia — synagogue first, then the Gentiles; stoned at Lystra and left for dead.

spans.label: Second journey
spans.detail: Philippi · Thessalonica · Berea · Athens · Corinth (18 months)
spans.note: Split with Barnabas; took Silas, picked up Timothy and Luke. Crossed into Europe at the Macedonian call — the Philippian jailer, the Areopagus, and a year and a half building the church at Corinth.

spans.label: Third journey
spans.note: Three years at Ephesus — the most fruitful and the most embattled — then back through Macedonia and Greece, gathering the collection for Jerusalem and setting his face toward it despite every warning.

spans.label: Caesarean custody
spans.note: Seized in the temple, nearly torn apart, then held two years at Caesarea — tried before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, until he appeals to Caesar.

spans.label: The voyage to Rome
spans.note: The great sea narrative — the northeaster, the cut anchors, the wreck on Malta, the viper that did not bite. Brought at last up the Appian Way.

spans.label: First Roman imprisonment
spans.note: Two years under guard in his own rented house, "proclaiming the kingdom of God… with all boldness, unhindered" — the word Acts chooses for its last.

spans.label: Release & final ministry
spans.aside: Beyond the end of Acts — reconstructed from the Pastorals and early tradition.
spans.note: If the Pastorals are read as Paul's, a release followed: further travel — Crete, Macedonia, perhaps the Spain he longed for — then a second arrest and the end.

spans.label: Galatians
spans.aside: Date contested: placed here on the early / South-Galatian view, just before the Jerusalem Council. On the later view it belongs c. A.D. 53–55.
spans.note: The freedom letter, white-hot — no gospel but the one received, no salvation by works of the law. Written to the churches of the first journey when teachers came demanding circumcision.

spans.label: 1–2 Thessalonians
spans.aside: During the second journey, soon after founding the church and sending Timothy back to it.
spans.note: Among the earliest Christian writing we have. Comfort for a young church grieving its dead and unsettled about the Lord's return.

spans.label: 1 Corinthians
spans.aside: From the long Ephesian stay of the third journey — "I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost."
spans.note: Answers to a divided, gifted, scandal-ridden church — factions, the Lord's table, the resurrection, and the more excellent way of love.

spans.label: 2 Corinthians
spans.aside: Written on the move through Macedonia after a painful visit and a tearful letter.
spans.note: The most personal letter — affliction and comfort, the treasure in clay jars, the thorn in the flesh, an apostle defending his weakness as the place God's power is shown.

spans.label: Romans
spans.aside: From Corinth at the end of the third journey, about to carry the collection to Jerusalem and hoping to reach Rome and then Spain.
spans.note: The fullest statement of the gospel — sin and grace, Jew and Gentile, the righteousness of God from faith for faith — written ahead to a church he had not yet seen.

spans.label: The Prison Epistles
spans.aside: Most likely from the Roman house-arrest of Acts 28 (some place Philippians, or all four, in an earlier Ephesian imprisonment).
spans.note: Letters from a prisoner — joy in Philippians, the runaway Onesimus in Philemon, the cosmic Christ in Colossians and Ephesians. Paul "an ambassador in chains."

spans.label: The Pastoral Epistles
spans.aside: Authorship and date are debated; if Paul's, they belong to the released ministry, 2 Timothy last of all, from a second imprisonment.
spans.note: To Timothy and Titus, on ordering the churches — and, at the very end, the valediction: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith."

events.label: The stoning of Stephen
events.note: Saul stands holding the coats and consenting to the death — the church's first martyr, and the first time we meet the man who will carry the gospel to the empire.

events.label: The Damascus road
events.note: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" The persecutor is struck blind and called — the apostle to the Gentiles, made by the risen Christ himself.

events.label: The Council of Jerusalem
events.note: The hinge of the whole story: the Gentiles need not be circumcised to belong. The freedom of the gospel secured in council, against the men who would have bound it to the law.

events.label: Before Gallio at Corinth
events.note: Dragged before the proconsul Gallio, who throws the case out. An inscription dates Gallio's term precisely — the one fixed point from which all of Paul's years are counted.

events.label: The riot at Ephesus
events.note: Demetrius and the silversmiths, whose idol trade the gospel threatens, fill the theater two hours deep: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

events.label: Arrest in Jerusalem
events.note: Seized in the temple on a false charge, nearly beaten to death, carried off by Roman soldiers. The journeys are over; the trials begin, and they will carry him to Rome.

events.label: Shipwreck off Malta
events.note: Fourteen nights driven before a northeaster, the grain ship broken on the rocks, all 276 aboard reaching land — and the prisoner, snake-bitten and unharmed, the calmest man on the beach.

events.label: Arrival in Rome
events.note: "And so we came to Rome." The gospel reaches the empire's heart — not in triumph but in chains, and preaching all the same.

events.label: Martyrdom under Nero
events.note: Beyond the close of Acts. Tradition holds that Paul was beheaded on the Ostian Way in Nero's persecution — "the time of my departure has come."

schemes.name: the Acts-based consensus
schemes.anchor: Gallio's proconsulship at Corinth · c. A.D. 51 (the Delphi inscription)
schemes.note: The standard reconstruction: Acts supplies the itinerary, the letters are slotted into it, and the whole is pinned to the one externally-dated point — Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12), fixed by an inscription at Delphi to about A.D. 51. From that peg the journeys and letters are counted forward and back.

schemes.name: Campbell · Framing Paul
schemes.anchor: the escape from the ethnarch of Aretas IV at Damascus · c. A.D. 36–37 (2 Cor 11:32–33)
schemes.note: Douglas Campbell (Framing Paul, 2014) brackets Acts and rebuilds the life from the letters alone, anchoring not on Gallio but on the flight from Aretas's ethnarch — the one window the Nabataeans plausibly held Damascus. The letters move early and reorder: 1–2 Thessalonians by c. 40, the captivity letters from an Ephesian (not Roman) imprisonment c. 50, and Galatians and Romans last, c. 51–52. The Pastorals he judges pseudonymous and drops; Acts' journey framework and everything after the letters fall outside the book's scope, so those blocks are removed rather than dated for him.

damascus-arabia.aside: The hinge of Campbell's whole chronology: the escape from Aretas's ethnarch (2 Cor 11:32–33) falls c. 36–37, the only plausible window of Nabataean control over Damascus. He counts from here, not from Gallio.

antioch-tarsus.aside: Campbell's long 'years of shadow' — a largely unsuccessful mission between the early Macedonian work and the Jerusalem conference. He does not map Acts' Tarsus-and-Antioch detail onto particular years.

second-journey.aside: Campbell splits what Acts fuses. The founding of the Macedonian churches — and so 1–2 Thessalonians — he dates to c. 40, roughly a decade before the consensus and before the conference. Acts' numbered-journey structure is set aside; the consensus 'first journey' is bracketed altogether.

third-journey.aside: Campbell's later Aegean and Asian phase, including an Ephesian imprisonment c. 50 — the setting, on his reading, of the captivity letters.

galatians.aside: Campbell dates Galatians LATE, not early — part of the 'year of crisis' with Philippians and Romans, c. 51–52. The reverse of the South-Galatian early dating shown under the consensus.

thessalonians.aside: Campbell's earliest letters, both authentic, c. 40–42 — written soon after the Macedonian founding.

romans.aside: Written last of the major letters, in the 'year of crisis,' c. 51–52.

prison-epistles.aside: Campbell's most striking move: Colossians, Ephesians (his 'Laodiceans') and Philemon come EARLY, c. 50, from an Ephesian imprisonment — before the Corinthian letters and Romans, inverting the usual late-Roman dating. (Philippians he groups later, with the 'year of crisis.')

damascus-road.aside: Three years before the Aretas escape (Gal 1:18). Reviewers rarely state Campbell's conversion year outright, so c. 34 is inferred from his 36–37 anchor.

gallio.aside: Campbell does not deny Paul was in Corinth c. 50–51, but he deliberately sets the Gallio synchronism aside — it is not load-bearing for him, as it is for the consensus.

ephesus-riot.aside: Correlated with the Ephesian imprisonment crisis that, on Campbell's reading, produced the captivity letters.

schemes.name: Lüdemann · Studies in Chronology
schemes.anchor: the relative time-spans of Galatians 1–2, counted from a crucifixion of A.D. 30
schemes.note: Gerd Lüdemann (Paul, Apostle to the Gentiles, 1984) builds only from the seven undisputed letters, anchoring on the spans Paul himself gives in Galatians 1–2 ('after three years… after fourteen years') counted from a crucifixion of A.D. 30. Acts is admitted only afterward, where it does not conflict. His signature result: the European churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth — are founded c. 38–41, about a decade before the consensus and before the Jerusalem conference, so 1 Thessalonians dates to c. 41. The deutero-Pauline letters (2 Thessalonians, Colossians, Ephesians, the Pastorals) and the post-collection Acts narrative are dropped.

damascus-arabia.aside: Conversion at Damascus in 33 (three years before the first Jerusalem visit, Gal 1:18), counted from a 30 A.D. crucifixion. The Aretas escape sits here too, but is not Lüdemann's anchor.

antioch-tarsus.aside: The years in Syria and Cilicia (Gal 1:21) after the first Jerusalem visit, until the European mission begins.

second-journey.aside: Lüdemann's signature claim: the independent European mission — Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth — dated to c. 38–41, about a decade earlier than the consensus and BEFORE the Jerusalem conference. Acts' numbered-journey order is set aside; the consensus 'first journey' is bracketed altogether.

third-journey.aside: The post-conference years gathering the collection through Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia, with Paul in Ephesus c. 51 (whence 1 Corinthians).

roman-imprisonment.aside: Only an indirect hint: Lüdemann allows that Philemon and Philippians may have been written from Rome c. 57. He reconstructs no house-arrest chronology.

galatians.aside: Written from Macedonia c. 52, alongside 2 Corinthians — late, not early.

thessalonians.aside: The famously early 1 Thessalonians, from Corinth c. 41. (2 Thessalonians Lüdemann judges deutero-Pauline and excludes.)

second-corinthians.aside: From Macedonia, c. 52 (chs. 1–9 and 10–13 taken together).

romans.aside: From Corinth, c. 53 — the latest of the undisputed letters in his scheme.

prison-epistles.aside: Only Philemon and Philippians count as genuine for Lüdemann (Colossians and Ephesians are excluded as deutero-Pauline); he places them at Ephesus c. 51–52 or, tentatively, at Rome c. 57.

damascus-road.aside: Conversion at Damascus, 33 — three years before the first Jerusalem visit (35), counted from a 30 A.D. crucifixion.

council.aside: Lüdemann's second Jerusalem visit, 48 — its outcome the collection pledge; the Antioch incident falls about here too.

gallio.aside: Lüdemann locates Paul in Corinth and Ephesus around 51, but does not make the Gallio inscription load-bearing; his framework is letter-internal.

arrest.aside: Lüdemann dates the third Jerusalem visit — to deliver the collection — to 54, the visit Acts says ended in arrest. His chronology effectively closes here.

rome-arrival.aside: Only the indirect 'from Rome c. 57' hint behind the prison letters; Lüdemann fixes no arrival narrative.
